meta.titre: Gas Exchange in Humans: breathing movements and the air sacs of the lungs
meta.sous_theme: Ventilation of the lungs, the structure of an air sac and the composition of breathed air

sections.contenu_markdown:
A footballer sprints on a football pitch in Limbe and soon breathes faster and deeper. After the match, his rate of breathing slowly returns to normal.
Behind this change are two separate things: the muscles that move air in and out of the lungs, and the thin surfaces where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it.
At the GCE, questions about breathing usually ask you to link the movements of the ribs and diaphragm to changes in volume and pressure, and the structure of the air sacs to their function.

items: Cells need oxygen for aerobic respiration, which releases carbon dioxide.
Blood carries gases around the body in the circulatory system.
Gas pressure falls when the volume of its container increases.

sections.titre: Breathing and gas exchange in the lungs
sections.contenu_markdown:
### The path of air
Air passes through the nose or mouth, the trachea, two bronchi, many bronchioles and ends in tiny air sacs called **alveoli**. The trachea is held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage. Its lining has cells with cilia and cells that make mucus; the mucus traps dust and bacteria and the cilia sweep it upwards.

### Breathing movements
| Feature | Inspiration (breathing in) | Expiration (breathing out) |
|---|---|---|
| Intercostal muscles | External muscles contract | External muscles relax |
| Ribs | Move up and out | Move down and in |
| Diaphragm | Contracts and flattens | Relaxes and curves upwards |
| Volume of the chest | Increases | Decreases |
| Pressure in the lungs | Falls below atmospheric pressure | Rises above atmospheric pressure |
| Movement of air | Air flows in | Air is forced out |

Air always moves from a region of higher pressure to one of lower pressure. So oxygen is brought into the lungs because the volume of the chest increases and the pressure in the lungs drops.

### Gas exchange in the alveoli
Oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveoli into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli. Alveoli are well suited to this because:
- there are millions of them, giving a very large surface area;
- their walls are only one cell thick, so the diffusion distance is short;
- they are moist, so gases dissolve;
- they are surrounded by a dense network of blood capillaries that carry the gases away;
- breathing keeps replacing the air, so the concentration gradient stays steep.

In the blood, oxygen combines with haemoglobin in red blood cells to form oxyhaemoglobin.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question compares the air breathed in with the air breathed out
variantes.contenu_markdown: Inhaled air contains about 21% oxygen and only a trace of carbon dioxide. Exhaled air contains about 16% oxygen and about 4% carbon dioxide, and more water vapour. Nitrogen stays about the same in both. The changes occur because the body uses oxygen in respiration and produces carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide turns limewater cloudy (milky), and exhaled air does so more quickly than inhaled air.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks about the effects of cigarette smoke
variantes.contenu_markdown: Smoke contains tar, which damages the cilia and lining of the airways and can cause cancer. It contains nicotine, an addictive drug, and carbon monoxide, which combines with haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen does and so reduces the oxygen carried by the blood.

sections.enonce_markdown: Describe what happens to the ribs, the diaphragm, the volume of the chest and the pressure in the lungs when a person breathes out quietly, and explain why air leaves the lungs.

etapes.justification: 'Describe' needs four events, and 'explain' needs the reason for the movement of air.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Four structures or quantities, followed by a reason.

etapes.justification: Breathing out is the opposite of breathing in.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The external intercostal muscles relax so the ribs move down and in; the diaphragm relaxes and curves upwards.

etapes.action: State the change in volume and pressure.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The volume of the chest decreases, so the pressure in the lungs rises above atmospheric pressure.

etapes.justification: Air flows from high pressure to low pressure.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Air is forced out of the lungs because the pressure inside is higher than outside.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Ribs move down and in; diaphragm relaxes and rises; chest volume decreases; lung pressure rises above atmospheric pressure, so air flows out from the high-pressure lungs to the lower pressure outside.

items.erreur_markdown: During inspiration the diaphragm relaxes and moves up.
items.pourquoi_faux: It is the other way round. In inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens, which increases the volume of the chest.
items.correction_markdown: Inspiration: diaphragm contracts and flattens; expiration: diaphragm relaxes and curves upwards.

items.erreur_markdown: Air is sucked into the lungs by the lungs themselves.
items.pourquoi_faux: The lungs have no muscle for breathing. The movement is caused by the intercostal muscles and the diaphragm, which change the volume and pressure of the chest.
items.correction_markdown: Muscles change the volume of the chest; the resulting pressure difference makes air flow in.

items.erreur_markdown: Humans breathe out only carbon dioxide.
items.pourquoi_faux: Exhaled air still contains about 16% oxygen, along with nitrogen, water vapour and about 4% carbon dioxide.
items.correction_markdown: Exhaled air has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than inhaled air, but it still contains oxygen.

items.erreur_markdown: Oxygen enters the blood by active transport in the alveoli.
items.pourquoi_faux: Oxygen enters the blood by diffusion down a concentration gradient, so no energy is needed.
items.correction_markdown: Gas exchange in the alveoli is by diffusion.

items.enonce_markdown: Name, in order, the parts of the respiratory system through which air passes from the nose to the place of gas exchange.

A resting student breathes 15 times in a minute, taking in about 500 cm³ of air in each breath. Inhaled air contains about 21% oxygen and exhaled air about 16%. (a) Calculate the volume of air breathed in each minute in dm³. (b) Assuming that the volume of a breath does not change, how much oxygen does the body take from one breath?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $15 \times 500 = 7\,500$ cm³ per minute, and $7\,500 \div 1\,000 =$ **7.5 dm³ per minute**.
(b) The percentage taken out is $21 - 16 = 5\%$, so the volume of oxygen is $\dfrac{5}{100} \times 500 =$ **25 cm³ per breath**.

items.enonce_markdown: Explain, in terms of structure, why the alveoli are an efficient surface for gas exchange, and say how exercise affects the rate of breathing and why.
items.solution_markdown:
Award a mark for each point. Many alveoli give a large surface area; their thin, one-cell-thick walls give a short diffusion distance; the moist lining lets gases dissolve; a close network of capillaries removes oxygen and brings carbon dioxide, which keeps the concentration gradient steep.
During exercise the rate and depth of breathing **increase**, because the muscles respire faster, use more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide, and the body must supply and remove more gas.

items_markdown: Air passes through the nose, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli; the trachea has cartilage rings and a lining of mucus and cilia.
Inspiration: intercostals and diaphragm contract, chest volume rises, pressure falls, air enters. Expiration is the reverse.
Alveoli have a large surface area, thin walls, a moist lining and a rich blood supply, and gases cross by diffusion.
Exhaled air has less oxygen (about 16%) and more carbon dioxide (about 4%) than inhaled air (about 21% oxygen).
Carbon monoxide in smoke combines with haemoglobin and reduces the oxygen carried by the blood.
